summary: Halfway Rescuer is an offline-first web app that helps astronauts assess their own health and act in an emergency when no doctor is aboard. It is inspired by the challenge scenario of a crewmate collapsing halfway to Mars. Its Emergency Protocol guides the rescuer one step at a time: check response, call the crew, check breathing, and run CPR with a live compression pacer and swap timer. It then builds a summary for Earth. A health console tracks eight indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen, temperature, glucose, sleep, mood and radiation. Each card explains how to measure it, why it matters in space, and what to do if a value looks abnormal, with colour-coded status and trend charts. A clickable body map links NASA’s five hazards to the body systems affected. A delay-tolerant outbox queues reports for Earth when the link is lost, with environment profiles for transit, station, Moon and Mars. All data is simulated and medical content is marked to be verified. It is a training prototype, not a medical device.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Halfway Rescuer is a website that helps astronauts when no doctor is on board. Its idea comes from the challenge video, where a crewmate suddenly collapses halfway to Mars and the person next to them has no medical experience.

If a crewmate collapses, the rescuer taps one big red button. The app then gives one simple instruction per screen: check if the person responds, call the crew, check breathing, and start CPR with a live beat to follow, a counter and a timer for swapping rescuers. At the end it builds a short summary for doctors on Earth.

The app also has a health console with eight indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen, temperature, blood sugar, sleep, mood and radiation. Each one explains how to measure it, why it matters in space, and what to do if the number looks wrong. Colours show green, amber or red, and charts show the trend. A clickable body figure shows how NASA’s five spaceflight hazards affect each body system.

Benefits

It guides people who are not doctors, works without internet, and saves a report for Earth even when the link is down.

Intended impact

The aim is that on long missions, astronauts can act quickly and safely, and that doctors on the ground get clear information. The same idea could help remote communities with little access to healthcare.

Tools used

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no backend), SVG and canvas for graphics, and the browser’s audio for the CPR beat. [Add the AI tools you used, for example Claude, because the form usually asks you to disclose them.]

How is it creative?

Most projects only show health numbers. Ours is built for the rescuer, step by step, in a real emergency. It also adds a delay-tolerant outbox for Earth, a clickable body map tied to NASA’s hazards, and a premium cinematic design.

What did the team consider?

Astronauts are not doctors, so every instruction is short and plain.

Earth help can be many minutes away, so the app works offline.

The medical thresholds are simple demo values, so we mark them “to be verified.”

All data is simulated, and the app says clearly that it is a training aid, not a medical device.

NASA’s hazards, Mars gravity and radiation facts come from NASA’s Human Research Program and the Canadian Space Agency.
